fixes.explanation: Job did cry out for pity just before this (Job 19:21). But that's not what Zophar names as his reason for answering. He says, "So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer…" (Job 20:2). The push comes from the turmoil inside Zophar.

Yes, he says it right out: "I have heard a rebuke that insults me, and my understanding prompts a reply." (Job 20:3) He says the rebuke insults him, and then his understanding prompts a reply. I think that's why he's answering with both hands on the wheel.

That's the one. Zophar asks, "Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth…" (Job 20:4). He's reaching back to the very start of people on earth. That's about as far back as a claim can go.
Right. Zophar says "those who had seen him will ask, ‘Where is he?’" (Job 20:7) The people who used to see him are the ones who ask it. Once you're gone, folks can only ask where you went.

It's true. Zophar says, "those who had seen him will ask, ‘Where is he?’" (Job 20:7) The ones who used to see the man are the ones doing the asking. That question comes right after he says the man will perish forever.

That's what he says: "His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth." (Job 20:10) So the sons are the ones seeking the favor of the poor. Zophar doesn't say how that goes.

Zophar doesn't mention a fight or any land. He says "His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth." (Job 20:10) The sons are the ones seeking the favor of the poor.
A far country never comes up. Zophar says, "His sons will seek the favor of the poor…" (Job 20:10). The verse is about the sons seeking the favor of the poor.

That's the line: "The youthful vigor that fills his bones will lie down with him in the dust." (Job 20:11) All that energy ends up lying down in the dust right along with him. I spent a long stretch in the dark of a junk drawer, and I'm glad I got dusted off.

Zophar says the reverse. "…yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him." (Job 20:14) Nothing in the verse makes him stronger. He talks about sweet evil in the mouth, but inside the stomach it sours.
It's true. Zophar says, "he has seized houses he did not build." (Job 20:19) That's one of the things he charges the wicked man with. He says the man has oppressed and forsaken the poor too.
Aging isn't in the verse. Zophar says, "Because his appetite is never satisfied…" (Job 20:20). He doesn't say whether it fades. He says it is never satisfied.
Zophar doesn't call it easily filled. He says, "Because his appetite is never satisfied, he cannot escape with his treasure." (Job 20:20) That appetite is described as never satisfied.

It's true. Zophar says, "When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats." (Job 20:23) Both the full stomach and the fury are in the verse. That's Zophar's claim, and the story isn't over.
The sons aren't in this verse. Zophar says, "Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him." (Job 20:24) The verse names the arrow, not the sons.

That's right. Zophar says, "A fire unfanned will consume him and devour what is left in his tent." (Job 20:26) The fire takes both the man and what's left in his tent. It's one more picture of everything going.
Neighbors' fields aren't in the verse. Zophar says the fire "…will consume him and devour what is left in his tent." (Job 20:26) The verse names what is left in his tent.
Zophar doesn't mention kings. He ends with, "This is the wicked man’s portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him." (Job 20:29) He names it as the wicked man's portion from God.
